meta.title: Live task updates, explained
meta.summary: Today the task board asks the server for changes every 10 seconds. This proposal pushes changes to open boards with server sent events instead. Taskflow and this proposal are fictional.

context.problem: Without push, a board learns about a teammate's change only on its next poll, up to 10 seconds later. Polling also makes most requests return nothing new.
goals: Changes show on open boards within one second
Fewer requests than polling at today's team sizes
Works through the corporate proxies our customers use
nonGoals: Collaborative editing of one task by two people
context.background: Board polls are 61 percent of API requests and 93 percent of them return no changes (October numbers from the RFC).

options.title: Keep polling, but slower
options.summary: Poll every 30 seconds to cut load.
cons: Changes take even longer to show

options.title: WebSockets
options.summary: A two way socket per open board.
pros: The client could send edits on the same socket
cons: Some customer proxies drop upgraded connections
Needs sticky sessions on the load balancer

options.title: Server sent events
options.summary: One long lived HTTP response per board that the server writes events to.
pros: Plain HTTP, so proxies treat it like a slow download
The browser reconnects on its own and resumes from the last event id
cons: One way only; edits still use normal requests
Browsers cap open connections per host over HTTP/1.1
options.why: Boards only need to hear about changes, not send on the same channel, so one way is enough; WebSockets would buy two way traffic we do not need at the cost of proxy failures.

diagrams.title: How the options score
diagrams.caption: Server sent events meet every goal except two way traffic, which boards do not need.

diagrams.title: Effort against impact
diagrams.caption: Server sent events give most of the gain of WebSockets for about half the work.

diagrams.title: What moves
diagrams.caption: Boards stop asking and start listening, and writes publish one event each.

items: A change shows up to 10 seconds late
Each board holds one event stream

items.label: Writes publish to Redis
items.detail: The task service publishes after the database commit.

items: A change shows in under a second

notes: Edits still use the normal tasks API.
Polling stays as the fallback when a stream cannot open.

nodes.label: Task board
nodes.summary: Shows a team's tasks and listens for changes.

nodes.label: Events endpoint
nodes.summary: Holds one open response per board and writes events to it.

nodes.label: Task service
nodes.summary: Saves the change, then publishes an event.

nodes.label: Redis pub/sub
nodes.summary: Fans one event out to every API instance with open streams.

flows.title: Seeing a teammate's change, today
flows.trigger: A teammate moves a task to Done
flows.summary: Your board finds out on its next poll.

steps.label: Saves the move
steps.detail: The teammate's edit is saved as today.

steps.label: Writes the task
steps.detail: The change is in Postgres now.

steps.label: Polls after up to 10 s
steps.detail: Your board asks again on its timer, not because anything changed.

steps.label: Returns the change
steps.detail: You see the move up to 10 seconds late.

flows.title: Seeing a teammate's change, proposed
flows.trigger: A teammate moves a task to Done
flows.summary: The change is pushed to your open board within a second.

steps.label: Publishes task.moved
steps.detail: One small event with the task id and new column.
steps.why: Publishing after the commit means a board never hears about a change that rolled back; publishing before would show ghosts.

steps.label: Delivers to every instance
steps.detail: Each API instance with open streams for that team gets it.

steps.label: Writes the event
steps.detail: Your board updates the card. Each event has an id, so a reconnect resumes where it left off.

risks.risk: Browsers cap HTTP/1.1 connections per host, so many tabs starve
risks.mitigation: Serve the stream over HTTP/2, where one connection carries many streams.

risks.risk: An event is lost while a board reconnects
risks.mitigation: Boards send Last-Event-ID; the endpoint replays the last 5 minutes from Redis.
Boards fall back to polling every 10 seconds, which is today's behavior.

rollout.label: Add the events endpoint behind a flag
Publish events from the task service
Turn it on for internal teams for one week
Turn it on for everyone, keep polling as fallback

quiz.question: A customer's proxy closes any response that stays open for 60 seconds. What does their board do?
options: Reconnects and resumes from the last event id
Stops updating until the page reloads
quiz.explain: The browser's EventSource reconnects on its own and sends the last event id, so nothing is lost. Falling back to WebSockets is tempting, but that option was not chosen and nothing in the design switches to it.

quiz.question: Boards show a task as Done, then it flips back a second later. Which step is likely in the wrong order?
quiz.explain: If the event goes out before the commit and the commit fails, boards show a change that never happened. Delivering to two instances is by design and cannot flip a task back.

quiz.question: You need boards to also show who is viewing them. Which part changes?
options: The events endpoint and the bus, with a new event type
quiz.explain: Presence is another event pushed to open boards, so it rides the same endpoint and bus. Changing only the board is tempting, but the board cannot learn about other viewers without the server telling it.

glossary.definition: A browser API where the server keeps one HTTP response open and writes events to it.
Asking the server for changes on a timer, whether or not anything changed.
Publishers send messages to a channel; every subscriber to that channel gets a copy.
